Leave number sixteen, Rue Louis-le-Grand, and continue towards the Opéra.

This time, take your time.

As the street opens out, the neighbourhood begins to change scale. The views become longer. The buildings become grander. And soon, the Palais Garnier starts to dominate the scene.

But there is something easy to forget. This magnificent vista has not always existed.

In the middle of the nineteenth century, the Paris you are walking through was much more tightly packed.

The new opera house was being built, but the great avenue intended to connect it with central Paris had yet to be opened all the way through.

Entire blocks had to vanish. Streets were cut through. Houses were demolished.

During the eighteen seventies, the photographer Charles Marville recorded that transformation. Among other things, he photographed the opening of the avenue between Rue Louis-le-Grand and Rue d'Antin.

In other words, almost exactly where you are walking now.

Try, for a moment, to remove the avenue from the view in front of you.

Imagine a much denser network of narrow streets. Building sites. Façades sliced open. Plots of land covered with demolition rubble.

That great straight road, which seems so natural today, had to be created.

Keep walking.

Now, we're changing periods once again. It is August, nineteen forty-four.

Paris is rising against the German occupation. Barricades appear. Police officers and members of the Resistance take action.

Across a city now in revolt, German positions come under growing pressure.

One of those positions lies directly ahead of you: the German command post near the Opéra, known as the Platzkommandantur.

Continue towards the Place de l'Opéra and Rue du Quatre-Septembre.

As you approach, find a safe place to stop without obstructing other pedestrians. Then turn and look towards the opera house.

We've arrived.

Now begin walking towards our final stop.

For the next few minutes, try to forget almost everything you can see around you.

The Palais Garnier disappears. The Avenue de l'Opéra disappears. The grand nineteenth-century buildings disappear.

Even several of the streets cease to exist in anything like their present form.

We are travelling back to sixteen fifty-two.

And Paris is not merely different in its architecture. The kingdom itself is in crisis.

Louis the Fourteenth is only thirteen years old. The Fronde is tearing France apart.

Princes. Great families. Parliament. Armies. Rival factions.

Alliances change. People negotiate, betray one another, make peace, and sometimes reach for their weapons.

As you walk, look at the oldest buildings that have survived in this part of Paris.

They seem old enough to us. Yet even they were built after the world we are about to enter.

Nearby once stood the great Hôtel de Vendôme.

Behind it stretched a much more open space than anything you see here today: a horse market.

Replace the façades in your imagination with rough, uneven ground, crowded with horses and traders, dust in the air and voices calling out during the busy hours of the day.

On the evening of the thirtieth of July, sixteen fifty-two, this place becomes the setting for an armed encounter.

Not to buy a horse. To fight.

Two men arrive here.

François de Vendôme, Duke of Beaufort.

And his brother-in-law, Charles-Amédée of Savoy, Duke of Nemours.

They belong to the same political camp. They belong to the same family.

And yet, just a few minutes later, one of them will be dead.
